blocks.content: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and only on the recommendation of the President.

rows: Either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha
Can amend, reject, or delay up to 6 months
Cannot reject or amend; can delay up to 14 days only

items: The decision of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha on whether a bill is a Money Bill or not is final and cannot be questioned in court or in either House.
There is no constitutional provision for a joint sitting in the case of a Money Bill or a Constitutional Amendment Bill.
Rajya Sabha can detain an Ordinary Bill for a maximum period of 6 months, but a Money Bill for only 14 days.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Bills introduced in Parliament are categorized into four types: Ordinary Bills, Money Bills, Financial Bills, and Constitutional Amendment Bills.
An Ordinary Bill can originate in either House of Parliament and requires a simple majority to pass.
Money Bills deal exclusively with financial matters listed under Article 110 and can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha with prior recommendation of the President.
The Rajya Sabha has limited powers regarding Money Bills; it cannot amend or reject them and must return them within 14 days.
Joint sittings under Article 108 are applicable to resolve deadlocks on Ordinary and Financial Bills, but not on Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills.
